blocks.content: FINAL & MOST DECISIVE PHASE OF FREEDOM STRUGGLE

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Government of India Act, 1935 established provincial autonomy and laid the constitutional framework for governance.
Congress Ministries ruled from 1937 to 1939, providing the leadership with its first major experience of administrative power.
Major wartime diplomatic steps included the August Offer (1940) and Cripps Mission (1942), both of which failed to resolve constitutional deadlocks.
The Quit India Movement (1942) and the armed struggle of Subhas Chandra Bose's INA dealt severe blows to British colonial authority.
The Mountbatten Plan and the Indian Independence Act of 1947 legally concluded British rule and led to the partition of the subcontinent.

blocks.content: 1. Introduction: Why 1934–1947 is the MOST CRUCIAL Phase

The period from 1934 to 1947 represents the final, most complex, and most decisive phase of the Indian National Movement. Unlike earlier phases which were dominated by mass agitations, this phase involved a combination of constitutional negotiations, mass uprisings, revolutionary activities, international pressures, and communal politics. British authority was seriously weakened during this period due to World War II, economic exhaustion, and growing resistance within India. The national movement during this phase was no longer about awakening political consciousness; it was about forcing the British to quit India permanently. This phase culminated in Independence and Partition in 1947.
2. Political Situation after 1934

After the withdrawal of the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1934, the Indian National Congress faced a critical situation. Continuous repression, imprisonment of leaders, and economic hardships had weakened mass movements temporarily. Gandhi withdrew from active politics to focus on constructive programmes, while Congress shifted towards constitutional methods without abandoning the goal of complete independence.
3. Government of India Act, 1935 – COMPLETE EXPLANATION

The Government of India Act, 1935 was introduced by the British as an attempt to stabilise their rule by granting limited autonomy while retaining real control. It was the longest and most detailed constitutional Act.

• Provincial Autonomy: Provinces were allowed to govern themselves without interference of Governors in normal matters.

• Abolition of Dyarchy in Provinces: Ministers were made responsible to legislatures.

• Dyarchy at Centre: Proposed but never implemented.

• Federal Structure: Planned federation of British India and princely states.

• Bicameral Legislatures: Introduced in some provinces.

• Federal Court: Established in 1937.

• Extended Franchise: Number of voters increased significantly.

Despite its reforms, the Act was seen as deeply flawed. Governors retained emergency powers, the centre remained under British control, and princely states were not democratised. Hence, the Act failed to satisfy nationalist aspirations.
4. Congress Ministries (1937–1939): First Experience of Power

Elections held under the 1935 Act in 1937 resulted in Congress forming ministries in 7 provinces. This period gave Indian leaders practical experience of governance and allowed them to implement pro-people policies.

• Reduction of land revenue and relief to peasants

• Promotion of primary and secondary education

• Release of political prisoners

• Protection of civil liberties

• Encouragement to local industries
When World War II broke out, Britain declared India a participant without consulting Indian leaders. Congress ministries resigned in protest, exposing the undemocratic nature of British rule.
5. Impact of World War II on Indian Politics

World War II critically weakened Britain economically and militarily. India was used as a major base for men and materials, increasing exploitation. At the same time, the war made Britain dependent on Indian cooperation.
6. August Offer (1940): Explained Clearly

The August Offer promised expansion of the Executive Council and future dominion status. However, it failed to assure full independence or immediate transfer of power, leading to its rejection by Congress.
7. Individual Satyagraha (1940–41)
Individual Satyagraha was launched by Gandhi to assert freedom of speech against India's forced participation in the war. It allowed limited protest while avoiding mass repression.
8. Cripps Mission (1942): Why It Failed

The Cripps Mission offered dominion status after the war and the right of provinces to secede. Congress rejected it due to absence of immediate power transfer, while the Muslim League objected to its provisions.
9. Quit India Movement (1942): FINAL MASS UPSURGE
The Quit India Movement was launched in August 1942 after the failure of the Cripps Mission. Gandhi's call of 'Do or Die' marked the final mass confrontation with British rule.

• Spontaneous mass participation

• Parallel governments in some regions

• Underground activities by leaders

• Brutal British repression
10. Subhas Chandra Bose & Indian National Army (INA)
Subhas Chandra Bose rejected Gandhian methods and believed that armed struggle was necessary. With Japanese support, he reorganised the INA to fight British rule.
INA trials united the nation, triggered protests, and weakened loyalty of Indian soldiers to British rule.
11. Cabinet Mission Plan (1946): Last British Attempt
The Cabinet Mission proposed a united India with a weak centre and strong provinces. While Congress accepted it with reservations, the Muslim League ultimately rejected it.
12. Direct Action Day (1946): Communal Turning Point
The Muslim League’s call for Direct Action Day resulted in massive communal violence, making partition appear inevitable.
13. Mountbatten Plan (1947): Road to Partition

items: Frequently tested: Chronological sequence of wartime initiatives — August Offer (1940) → Individual Satyagraha (1940–41) → Cripps Mission (1942) → Quit India Movement (1942).
Pay attention to the key differences between the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) and Mountbatten Plan (1947) regarding Indian unity versus partition.
Focus on key features of the Government of India Act 1935: Dyarchy at the Center, Provincial Autonomy, and proposed All-India Federation.

blocks.content: The Mountbatten Plan proposed immediate transfer of power and partition of India. Faced with chaos and violence, Congress accepted partition as the only viable option.
14. Indian Independence Act, 1947 – LEGAL END OF BRITISH RULE
The Act formally ended British authority and created two independent dominions – India and Pakistan. It marked the culmination of nearly 200 years of colonial rule.
15. Overall Significance of 1934–1947 Phase

This phase brought together mass struggle, revolutionary action, and constitutional negotiations. It destroyed the foundations of British imperialism and fulfilled the long-cherished dream of freedom.
16. SSC One-Liners & High-Probability Questions
Govt of India Act – 1935 | Congress Ministries – 1937 | Quit India – 1942 | INA – Subhas Bose | Cabinet Mission – 1946 | Mountbatten Plan – 1947 | Independence – 15 August 1947
